name: Viking 1 Lander
objective: First successful Mars surface operation. Biology experiments to search for life, meteorology, seismology, and soil analysis.
description: Viking 1 was NASA's first successful Mars lander. It touched down in Chryse Planitia and operated for over six years, returning the first colour images from the Martian surface and conducting biology experiments searching for signs of life. Contact was lost on 13 November 1982.

name: Viking 2 Lander
objective: Biology experiments, meteorology, seismology, and soil analysis at a higher-latitude site than Viking 1.
description: Viking 2 landed in Utopia Planitia at a higher latitude than Viking 1, returning images, weather data, and biology experiment results. It operated until battery failure on 11 April 1980.

name: Mars Pathfinder (with Sojourner Rover)
objective: Demonstrate low-cost Mars landing with airbags; deploy Sojourner rover to study rocks and soil; atmospheric and weather measurements.
description: Mars Pathfinder used an innovative airbag-cushioned landing system in Ares Vallis. The Carl Sagan Memorial Station (lander) and Sojourner micro-rover operated until loss of contact on 27 September 1997, far exceeding the planned 30-day mission. Sojourner became NASA's first Mars rover.

name: Mars Exploration Rover A — Spirit
twinMission: Opportunity Rover — twin Mars Exploration Rover
objective: Investigate geological history of water in Gusev Crater; characterise soil and rocks.
description: Spirit landed inside Gusev Crater and explored the terrain for over six years, far exceeding its 90-sol design life. It discovered compelling evidence that Mars was once wetter. Spirit became stuck in soft soil in May 2009 and NASA declared the mission over on 25 May 2011 after losing contact.

name: Mars Exploration Rover B — Opportunity
twinMission: Spirit Rover — twin Mars Exploration Rover
objective: Investigate geological evidence of past water activity in Meridiani Planum.
description: Opportunity landed in Eagle Crater and operated for nearly 15 years — the longest-running Mars surface mission to date. It found definitive evidence that liquid water once existed on Mars. Contact was lost on 10 June 2018 during a global dust storm. NASA declared the mission over on 13 February 2019.

name: Phoenix Mars Lander
objective: Study the history of water and habitability potential of the Martian arctic soil; confirm presence of water ice.
description: Phoenix used a propulsive landing near the Martian north pole and directly confirmed the presence of water ice when its thrusters exposed the icy subsurface. It also detected perchlorate in the soil. The lander succumbed to the Martian winter; its mission ended in November 2008.

name: Mars Science Laboratory — Curiosity
objective: Assess whether Mars ever had an environment capable of supporting microbial life; study climate and geology.
description: Curiosity landed using the sky-crane descent system in Gale Crater. It confirmed ancient Mars had the conditions to support microbial life and continues to operate as of 2026, climbing Mt. Sharp (Aeolis Mons). It is the heaviest rover ever landed on Mars.

name: InSight Mars Lander
objective: Study the interior structure and thermal state of Mars using seismometer and heat probe.
description: InSight (Interior Exploration using Seismic Investigations, Geodesy and Heat Transport) used a seismometer (SEIS) to detect over 1,300 marsquakes and study Mars' interior layers. Its heat probe (HP3) could not penetrate the regolith as planned. Contact was lost on 15 December 2022 as dust covered its solar panels.

name: Mars 2020 — Perseverance
objective: Search for signs of ancient microbial life; collect rock and regolith samples for future Earth return; demonstrate oxygen production from CO₂ (MOXIE); deploy Ingenuity helicopter.
description: Perseverance landed in Jezero Crater, an ancient lake delta, and is NASA's most capable rover to date. It carries the MOXIE experiment (Mars oxygen production), the Ingenuity helicopter, and advanced instruments for astrobiology. It has collected dozens of scientifically important rock cores for the planned Mars Sample Return mission.

name: Mars Polar Lander
objective: Land near Mars south pole and study volatiles and climate history in polar layered deposits.
description: Mars Polar Lander was lost on descent on 3 December 1999. The probable cause was spurious signals from the landing leg sensors that caused the descent engines to cut off prematurely before touchdown. Its companion Deep Space 2 microprobes also failed.
